senses.gloss: To grow or increase very quickly, especially in business.
examples: Tourism *boomed* after the new airport opened.
Sales *boom* every December and die off in January.
The town has been *booming* since the plant reopened.

senses.gloss: To lift someone by pushing them from below.
examples: Her brother *boosted* her onto the wall.
*Boost* me a little higher — I still can't reach the branch.
He was *boosting* the kids onto his shoulders one at a time.

senses.gloss: To kick something hard.
examples: The kicker *booted* a 48-yard field goal.
He *boots* the ball farther than anyone on the team.
She was *booting* an empty can along the sidewalk.

senses.gloss: To make a deep round hole in something with a tool.
examples: They *bored* a hole through the wall for the cable.
The company *bores* wells for drinking water.
Crews have been *boring* a tunnel under the river since spring.

senses.gloss: (of a check) To be sent back unpaid because there is not enough money in the account.
senses.ru: не проходить, вернуться без оплаты (о чеке)
examples: His rent check *bounced* last month.
If a payment *bounces*, the bank charges a fee.
Two of their checks have *bounced* this year.

senses.gloss: To fight with the fists as a sport.
examples: He *boxed* in college and still trains twice a week.
They *box* three rounds on Friday night.
She has been *boxing* since she was twelve.

senses.gloss: To label someone publicly as something bad, so that the name sticks.
senses.ru: клеймить, заклеймить; объявлять (лжецом и т. п.)
examples: The press *branded* him a liar.
One bad season can *brand* a player for years.
Nobody wants to be *branded* a cheat.

senses.gloss: To give a product or a company a name, a look, and an image that customers recognize.
senses.ru: брендировать, создавать бренд; продвигать под маркой
examples: The agency *branded* the new coffee chain.
They *brand* everything in the same shade of green.
The app is *branded* as a tool for teachers.

senses.gloss: To break a law, a contract, or an agreement.
examples: The company *breached* the contract by missing the deadline.
Sharing the file would *breach* the agreement.
He has *breached* the terms of his parole twice.

senses.gloss: (of trouble or a storm) To build up slowly and be about to happen.
examples: A storm was *brewing* over the mountains all afternoon.
Resentment *brewed* quietly for years before anyone spoke up.
Trouble *brews* every time the budget comes up.

senses.gloss: To clean, smooth, or groom something with a brush.
examples: *Brush* your teeth before bed.
She *brushed* her hair and grabbed her coat.
He has been *brushing* the dog all afternoon.

senses.gloss: To bend or give way out of shape under weight or heat.
examples: Cheap sheet metal *buckles* in the sun.
His knees *buckled* when he heard the news.
The rails had *buckled* in the heat and the train stopped.

senses.gloss: To hide a small microphone somewhere in order to listen in secret.
senses.ru: прослушивать; ставить жучок, устанавливать подслушивающее устройство
examples: The FBI *bugged* the hotel room.
He was sure someone had *bugged* his phone.
They spent weeks *bugging* the suspect's office.

senses.gloss: To sell or supply several products together as one package.
senses.ru: продавать в комплекте, объединять в пакет
examples: The laptop comes *bundled* with antivirus software.
The cable company *bundles* internet and TV.
They *bundled* the two courses and dropped the price.

senses.gloss: To pat a baby on the back so that it brings up swallowed air.
examples: *Burp* the baby before you put her down.
He *burped* the twins one after the other.
She was *burping* the baby when the phone rang.

senses.gloss: To put a dead body in the ground or in a tomb at a funeral.
examples: They *buried* him next to his wife.
The family will *bury* her on Saturday.
He is *buried* in a small cemetery outside town.

senses.gloss: To ruin something by doing it clumsily or badly.
examples: The waiter *butchered* my last name.
Don't *butcher* the song — practice it first.
They have *butchered* a perfectly good script.

senses.gloss: To be full of noise, talk, and excitement.
examples: The restaurant was *buzzing* on Saturday night.
The newsroom *buzzed* with rumors all morning.
Downtown *buzzes* until two in the morning.

senses.gloss: To hide a supply of something in a safe or secret place.
examples: Squirrels *cache* nuts all over the yard.
He *cached* a spare key under the porch.
The rebels had *cached* weapons in the hills.

senses.gloss: To give someone or something a name, or to use a particular name for them.
examples: They *called* the baby Maya.
What do you *call* this in English?
The street was once *called* Mill Road.

senses.gloss: To order something official to take place and summon people to it.
examples: The governor *called* a special session.
The union has *called* a strike for Monday.
The coach *calls* a timeout with a minute left.

senses.gloss: To cover the top of something with a cap or a lid.
senses.ru: закрывать крышкой, закупоривать, закупорить; надевать колпачок
examples: *Cap* the bottle tightly before you shake it.
She *capped* her pen and closed the notebook.
The old well has been *capped* since 2019.

senses.gloss: (of a store) To keep a product in stock for sale.
senses.ru: иметь в продаже, держать в ассортименте
examples: Do you *carry* size 11?
The pharmacy *carries* the same brand for less.
They stopped *carrying* that model last year.

senses.gloss: To have a disease or a gene in your body and be able to pass it on.
examples: Mosquitoes *carry* the virus.
She *carries* the gene but has no symptoms.
The ticks were *carrying* Lyme disease.

senses.gloss: To have something as an attached result or penalty.
examples: The charge *carries* a five-year sentence.
The surgery *carried* a real risk of infection.
It is a felony *carrying* a fine of up to $10,000.

senses.gloss: To warn someone that something may be dangerous or unwise.
examples: Police *cautioned* drivers to stay off the roads.
I would *caution* against signing anything today.
Doctors have long *cautioned* that the drug is addictive.

senses.gloss: To praise and honor someone or something publicly.
examples: The exhibit *celebrates* the women who built the railroad.
His novels *celebrated* ordinary working people.
She has been *celebrated* as one of the great cellists of her generation.

senses.gloss: To become different, or to make something different.
examples: The town has *changed* a lot in ten years.
Nothing I said *changed* his mind.
The climate is *changing* faster than anyone expected.

senses.gloss: To take something away and put a fresh or new one in its place.
senses.ru: менять, поменять (постель, шину, подгузник); заменять, заменить
examples: I need to *change* the sheets.
He *changed* the tire in the rain.
Who's *changing* the baby?

senses.gloss: To exchange money for the same value in another currency or in smaller bills.
examples: Where can I *change* dollars into pesos?
She *changed* a twenty at the register.
We had our money *changed* at the airport.

senses.gloss: To direct money, effort, or feeling toward one particular purpose.
examples: She *channeled* her grief into her work.
The city *channels* most of the tax money into schools.
Funds were being *channeled* through a small charity.

senses.gloss: To accuse someone formally of a crime.
examples: Police *charged* him with fraud.
Prosecutors will *charge* both drivers.
She has been *charged* with two counts of theft.

senses.gloss: To put electricity into a battery.
examples: *Charge* your phone before the flight.
The battery *charges* in about an hour.
I left the laptop *charging* overnight.

senses.gloss: To rush forward in attack.
examples: The bull *charged* the fence.
Fans *charged* onto the field after the final whistle.
He came *charging* into the room without knocking.

senses.gloss: To plan a route or a course of action.
examples: The captain *charted* a course around the storm.
The new director wants to *chart* a different course for the museum.
They are still *charting* their next move.

senses.gloss: (of teeth) To knock together quickly because of cold or fear.
examples: His teeth were *chattering* by the time we got inside.
My teeth *chattered* all the way home.
Her teeth *chatter* whenever she climbs out of the pool.
